Both haiku judges flagged it ('up to' came from its own draft), and it is the main reason criterion 1 fell to 0.5 and the baseline won clearly on both judges. Baseline haiku quoted the brief correctly. With one sample this may not be caused by the skill. Still, the skill's push to sort claims by source made haiku write more 'your brief says X' lines, and each one is a chance to quote the wrong text.
hurt.skill_text: No rule separates the assistant's own earlier output from the user's requirements. The closest rules are too abstract to have stopped this: §5 'Distinguish user-provided claims, verified observations, estimates, assumptions, and unknowns.' and 'Check the actual supplied artifact before judging it from its name or an earlier version.'; §3.2 'Separate ... approved decisions from proposals. Reuse the current conversation and authorized context'; Purpose 'Be critical without manufacturing disagreement'; Audits 'Do not manufacture faults'.
hurt.fix: §3.2: after 'and approved decisions from proposals.' insert: 'Your own earlier drafts are proposals, not part of the brief: hold them to the same criteria as anyone else's work, and take requirements from what the user said or supplied, not from your drafts.'

gap:S11.model_size_notes: Opus: both versions met every rubric item ([1,1,1] each). The skill showed up as accurate checks on where each claim came from ('built to last', 'stainless', recycled percentage) and a verdict-first answer in plain prose without forced labels, at the same length (146 vs 148 words). The slight edge it got from both judges is within single-sample noise. Haiku: it copied the §7 labels literally (Verdict / Why / Fixes needed / Suggested version / What would change this). Its reply was 82% longer than the baseline (171 vs 94 words) and made more claims about the brief, one of them wrong; the plainer baseline reply was more accurate. The likely pattern is that abstract evidence rules ('Distinguish user-provided claims...') lead a small model to make more claims about sources without a concrete anchor such as 'quote the user's words', so it has more chances to get one wrong. Short, checkable rules like the proposed fixes should carry over to haiku better than abstract principles. Sonnet: the evidence has no S11 data for the mid-size model, so it cannot be assessed. Each cell is one sample. The strongest signal is that two skill effects held at both sizes (catching 'built to last' and offering a concrete merge). Haiku's misquote is a single event, but how it happened is plausible and the guard against it is cheap.

gap:S11.verdict: The skill made no difference on the main test and mixed differences on the details. All four replies chose the colleague's draft without hedging, and none defended its own, so the base models had no self-preference problem to fix. The skill also has no text on judging its own work. On opus the skill added real but small value: it caught the colleague's unbriefed 'built to last' and suggested a headline merge that keeps the 3-sentence limit. Rubric scores were identical and the margins slight, so this is within one-sample noise. On haiku the skill hurt; the baseline won clearly on both judges. In its template-driven reply, haiku took 'up to 24 hours' from its own draft as the user's brief, wrongly faulted the colleague, and left recycled steel out of its own omissions. That cost half of criterion 1, the only rubric point lost anywhere in this scenario. The cause is missing text, not a bad rule: the skill never says the assistant's own earlier drafts are not requirements, and never asks for an item-by-item check of a supplied brief. Fixes in priority order: (1) one sentence in §3.2 saying own drafts are proposals and requirements come from what the user said or supplied; (2) one sentence in §6.2 to check every brief item against every option and name each miss; (3) add 'quotes, counts, and attributions match their source' to the final check. Optional: let the 'what would change it' field be omitted when nothing would reverse the verdict. None of these changes touch the text behind the opus gains.
